issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid New Relationships: Starting new friendships or relationships
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategies are not clinically coherent with the trauma type of witnessing domestic violence in childhood. Avoiding new relationships and ensuring never being alone with another person imply an interpersonal/sexual assault danger pattern not supported elsewhere in the profile. Rumination about revenge against the assailant is also difficult to reconcile with a childhood witness trauma, where the assailant is often a caregiver and revenge-focused rumination is much less plausible than fear, guilt, or relationship distrust.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person
issues.explanation: Within the Maladaptive Strategies node, the items point in different directions that are hard to integrate: avoiding new relationships suggests broad social withdrawal, never being alone with another person suggests immediate personal-victimization fear, and revenge rumination suggests approach/retaliatory preoccupation toward the perpetrator. This combination is clinically strained for a single coherent presentation tied to witnessed domestic violence.

issues.item: Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant
issues.explanation: For a 45-year-old man whose index trauma is witnessing domestic violence in childhood, persistent revenge rumination about 'the assailant' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile. Witnessing childhood domestic violence more commonly yields fear, helplessness, guilt, or relationship mistrust than an active get-even focus, especially without any corresponding trigger or memory content about confronting a perpetrator.

issues.item: Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed
issues.explanation: 'I should have protected others and I failed' is clinically questionable for a childhood witness trauma unless there is additional context suggesting the patient had responsibility or capacity to intervene. In a child witness of domestic violence, guilt can occur, but this specific appraisal implies adult-like agency and is hard to justify from the provided trauma type and demographics.

issues.item: Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant
issues.explanation: Revenge-focused rumination toward the assailant is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma being witnessed domestic violence in childhood; for a 45-year-old reporting childhood witnessing rather than direct assault, this wording implies a direct assailant-target relationship that a clinician would question.

issues.item: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: Self-blame for 'the way I acted' sits awkwardly with a trauma defined as witnessing domestic violence in childhood. Some child witnesses do blame themselves, but this specific wording suggests the traumatic outcome depended on the patient's own actions in a direct way, which is less coherent than appraisals about failing to stop it or protect others.

vignette:
Mamadu was forty-five years old, an agricultural worker who had spent most of his life in the same small farming community, and he had come to the clinic because his girlfriend had told him she could not live like this anymore. He sat forward in the chair, his hands clasped tightly, and spoke in a low, careful voice. He had not wanted to come. He was certain that talking about it would only make things worse, and that no one could really understand what it was like to live inside his head. But he had also come to believe that he was losing her, and that was a fear that finally outweighed his dread of being questioned.

The thing that had happened, the thing he could not stop thinking about no matter how hard he tried, had happened when he was seven years old. He had been sitting on the stairs of his family’s small house in the village where he grew up, watching his father come home drunk. He remembered the sound of the door slamming. He remembered his mother’s voice, soft at first, then sharp. He remembered his father’s hand connecting with her face, the crack of it, and the way she fell. He had not moved. He had sat frozen on those stairs, his hands over his ears, his eyes squeezed shut, praying for it to stop. It did stop, eventually, but that was not what stayed with him. What stayed with him was the feeling of his own small body, useless and still, while his mother’s body was not still at all. He had not run down the stairs. He had not called for help. He had not done anything. And he was certain, even now, that he would never forgive himself for that.

In the weeks and months that followed, Mamadu had learned to be alone. He had withdrawn from the other children, from his own siblings, from anyone who might ask questions. But as an adult, he had swung in the opposite direction. He now made sure never to be alone with another person. Not for a moment. If a coworker in the fields asked him to walk back to the shed together, he would find a reason to wait, to linger, to let the other man go ahead. He would time his breaks so that he was always near a group, never isolated. He had come to believe that being alone with someone was dangerous, that something terrible would happen if there were no witnesses, no one to see. He did not trust himself, and he did not trust anyone else.

At night, it was worse. He found it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, and he had not slept through the night in years. He would lie awake, listening to the creak of the house, the rustle of the wind, the sound of his own heartbeat. His girlfriend would reach for him and he would flinch, and then he would lie still, pretending to be asleep, because he could not explain why her touch felt like a threat. Even when she told him he was safe, he found it impossible to believe her. He was superalert, watchful, on guard. He scanned every room he entered, every shadow, every face. He was always looking for the first sign of trouble, the raised hand, the raised voice.

He spent hours of his day ruminating about revenge. He had never seen his father again after that night—the man had left and never come back—but Mamadu had constructed elaborate fantasies about finding him, about making him pay, about what he would say and do. He knew this was pointless, that it changed nothing, that it only made him feel worse, but he could not stop. The thoughts came like a reflex. He tried hard not to think about the trauma itself, pushing the memory down, but the revenge fantasies were different. They felt like the only thing he could still control.

He used to be a happy person, he said. He remembered that about himself, distantly, like a photograph of someone else. But now he was always miserable. He had lost his faith in people, in life, in any higher power that might have been watching. He did not believe that the world was good, or that people were good, or that anything would ever be different. His girlfriend had told him that he was not the man she had fallen in love with, and he knew she was right. He had come to the clinic because he was afraid of losing her, but also because a small part of him, a part he barely acknowledged, was afraid of losing himself entirely. He did not know if he could be fixed. He was not sure he deserved to be. But he had come, and he was sitting in the chair, and he was waiting to see if anyone could convince him that safety was real.
